Michael Beary

Michael Beary

Michael Beary  

This excellent book should rest on the book-shelves of every therapist treating women clients. It is written by an established authority in the field of eating disorders who has written other books on the subject including Fat is a Feminist Issue which is a classic. The strength of this new work rests on the evident wealth of experience that the author has of patients battling to free themselves from the grip of anorexia nervosa. She has a lucid and articulate style which makes the book available to both professionals and the lay public.

She has had little experience of people suffering from bulimia and wisely avoids anything other than passing reference to this problem which increasingly is requiring help from therapists skilled in that area. Her analyses of the patients she describes are thorough, intuitive and in agreement with the conclusions of other experts. For those of us who like to see our patients' dis-ease in terms of psychological development, family relations and social pressures it is easy to agree with her that genetic biochemical and neuro-endocrine explanations are inappropriate. In fact I suspect we dismiss some truth in the process.

There are two important new theses in this book, one I heartily endorse and the other about which I have reservations.

Peter Hill

Peter Hill

Peter Hill  

Handicapping anxiety in childhood is virtually always managed by psychological methods and rightly so. Over the last decade the principal developments in such treatment have largely been behavioural or derived from whole family treatments. Matching attachment theory to clinical observation has become a commonplace endeavour in formulation and delineation of the natural and normal history of childhood fears is firmly established as a research activity though as yet incomplete.

Little in this small multi-author book reflects this. Barker provides a sensible but low-key chapter on assessment and family dysfunction. Likewise Herbert comments on behavioural management in appropriate but general terms. There is a useful chapter by Burton on anxiety produced by physical illness and treatments but otherwise the contributions could have been written at any time in the last forty years. Some offerings are frankly quaint.

The editor does not contribute and, alas, does not appear to have harnessed his contributors to plough any consistent furrow. In particular no recognisable definition of anxiety emerges. I am not sure who this book is intended for; I doubt it will enlighten readers of this Journal.

Peter Hill

[[RunningHead]]

Applying the Social Psychology of Groups in Clinical Settings

R. Fielding and S. Llewelyn

S. Llewelyn

S. Llewelyn  

The basic proposition to be explored in this paper is that psychotherapists currently make inadequate use of social psychology's knowledge of the principles of group dynamics and the ‘groupy’ aspects of behaviour, both in understanding an individual's behaviour and problems, and in applying that knowledge to their clinical practice. We are thus hoping to continue the debate opened by Brehm (1976), Feldman and Orford (1980), Weary and Mirels (1982) and others, all of whom suggest that this form of cross-fertilisation could enrich a number of applied disciplines, particularly those which practise psychotherapy. Coupled with this we also recognise the fact that social psychology itself is limited in its appreciation of group phenomena, having become more and more interested in the individual within a group rather than the group per se (see Steiner 1974, for a discussion of the decline of the group in social psychology). This is however outside the scope of the current paper, in which we will simply focus upon the theories and practices of psychotherapists.

The most obvious use of a ‘group’-type analysis is of course group therapy. The level of analysis most often used is that of the individual; an individual who just happens to exist for the moment in a group setting. Thus such an analysis focuses on either the intrapersonal or the inter-personal aspects of that individual's behaviour. In recent years there has been an upsurge in the interest shown by health care professionals in the use of group methods (for instance, Friedman 1979, Scheidlinger 1984a). Parallel with this interest is an awareness of the stresses and difficulties involved in operating within groups. This possibly reflects a respect for the power of group phenomena: a power which can be used and experienced as both negative and positive. Yet possibly because of this awareness of the power and riskiness of operating on a group level, and also because of the absence of adequate theories which are immediately appealing to the clinician, many psychotherapists repeatedly revert to the (merely) individualistic level of analysis. (This has been discussed in more detail by Buss 1975, Gergen 1973, Sampson 1977, Kelly and Llewelyn 1980, and others.)

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary by a Member of the “B” Group of Psychoanalysts

Geraldine Fitzpatrick

Geraldine Fitzpatrick

Geraldine Fitzpatrick  

In this clinical commentary I shall attempt to construct various hypotheses from the available material. I am interested in the patient's life story and the pattern of her relationships repeated through her childhood, in adult life and now with her therapist. I also ask ‘why does she present for therapy now?’

The vignette suggests a very difficult treatment during which the therapist must endure powerful countertransference feelings: I would make the transference and countertransference analysis a principal focus of the treatment, even though this is a twice-weekly psychotherapy. I note that this is still the early stages of treatment and I would expect a considerable testing out of the therapist and treatment alliance.

Family Background

For the first two years of her life, this woman had an exclusive relationship with her mother. This potentially could have been a positive experience, but she reports her mother to have been frustrating and unfulfilling and I would imagine this to be the basis of a strong narcissistic rage that has come to dominate her life. Both parents appear to have been psychologically absent and not ‘good enough’. Her mother never treated her in a positive way. Her father was violent when present. Neither parent encouraged her to see herself as worthy, likeable, or able to be cared about.

Indeed she externalises and reverses this process, attempting to protect and care for others: however, she is unsuccessful in this and the failure of this defence mechanism must be an additional narcissistic blow to her. A likely additional source of her narcissistic rage was having to share her mother with her father and sister in turn, and these multiple rejections seem to have led to repeated failures to sustain relationships through her life.

Some possible pointers to ‘why now?’ are that she is approaching her menopause and her daughter (the longest-lasting of her adult relationships) is approaching puberty and adolescence - i.e. a sexual life of her own, and increasing separateness from her mother. although the apparent precipitant of the symptoms is the break-up of her relationship with Dave, I would also wonder whether there might have been a critical event in her extended family (that is, the patient's mother or father).

Rugby Psychotherapy Conference 1986

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

(Working Party Chairman, Rugby Psychotherapy Conference), c/o Lincoln Clinic and Institute, 77 Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7HS

Michael Pokorny  

We met from the 10th-12th January, 1986 at Stanford Hall Co-operative College in Leicestershire and had an interesting and constructive Conference which has brought us another step nearer to formulating coherent ideas about bringing psychotherapy practitioners and their organisations together in a formal way. In view of what had happened last year and the year before, this Conference was conducted mainly in plenary sessions and the actual content of the Constitution was the bread and butter of the meetings having, in the past, been rather relegated to Sunday morning when there has not been that much time.

We had the usual Friday evening talk followed by discussion. This time it was on the question of the so-called core professions and their relationship to psychotherapy which, of course, also raises the question of whether or not it would be a good idea for psychotherapy to form itself into a distinct and separate profession. In discussing the Constitution, we essentially found that broadly speaking the fourth draft Constitution is widely acceptable and that the issue now is one of precisely what kind of structure we want for the Standing Conference. On a straw poll we found interestingly that, although a minority of us were actually mandated to commit our organisations, just over half felt their organisations would join the Standing Conference as presently formulated and of the remainder half thought their organisations would not and the other half actually did not know. This led us to discussions of just what kind of structure might be more widely acceptable and I discovered during the course of this that I had got very hooked on to the notion of a single unifying professional identity which is not actually the majority view and which, if stuck to too vigorously, could even hold up the progress of the Conference.

What we need to ask our member organisations now is what level of federal structure they are looking for, what degree of autonomy amongst the Membership they feel is appropriate. And the next question is whether the Constitution is acceptable as it is and if it isn't the Membership should' offer specific written statements as to what they would like to see instead. One issue that was raised repeatedly in a variety of forms was the relationship of a possible emerging profession of psychotherapy with other existing professions to which most psychotherapists already belong and to other professional organisations which have bearing upon but are not specifically or even mainly concerned about the practise of psychotherapy, such as the Royal College of Psychiatrists. The Working Party was interestingly expanded for the forthcoming year to the twelve that is recommended in the Constitution as the appropriate number so it is as though we have a Standing Conference Working Party in embryo that has been elected even though the Standing Conference is still quite some way from inauguration. Our brief for the next year was quite clear.

Love and Narcissism in Psychoanalytic Practice edited by Herbert S. Strean. Published by The Haworth Press: New York 1985.

Janet Boakes

Janet Boakes

Janet Boakes  

This is a curiously uneven little book. First published as an issue of Current Issues in Psychoanalytic Practice in 1985 it is reprinted in this form. It is a collection of papers on Narcissism from a classical psychoanalytic position. There is no mention of either Kernberg or Kohut, both of whom have made major contributions to the subject. It suffers from lack of this perspective.

Overall the book with its very specific approach is likely to appeal to a relatively narrow readership. To those versed in psychoanalysis it will probably be absorbing, but to non-analysts it lays itself open to the stricture of saying more about the working of the analytic mind than of the subject it addresses. As such it still makes intriguing reading. The editor's aim is to combine ‘scholarship with humanism’ and the approach is a mixture of extended case presentation and theoretical papers.

The first paper is a lengthy case presentation of severe obsessional disorder with discussion by Joyce McDougall. Though heavily analytic it does present a fascinating account of the analysis of an intractable problem. Whether the patient derived much benefit remains at best unclear.

The second paper by Reuben Fine, unfortunately titled ‘Academy of Love’, which proved to be a quote from Freud, presents a fascinating look at ‘Love’ from philosophical, historical, sociological, ethological and clinical perspectives. For this well-written and fascinating paper alone I am glad to have read the book.

There is a practical down-to-earth paper on psychotherapy with adolescents, full of wisdom and written by a man who clearly understands and likes adolescents. This paper had useful, practical hints on engaging adolescents, on countertransference, besides other issues such as dealing with parents. This paper and the one on ‘Love’ are by far the most readable and generally interesting.

The rest of the book includes an appreciation and application of the work of Edith Jacobson, a good introduction to her ideas, and a paper on ‘the automobile as a narcissistic object’ which suffers from the same handicap as the first in being too specialised in its approach. Nevertheless it makes intriguing reading. The final paper is a review of a book on Reagan and American politics that says a good deal more about the author than it probably does about either Reagan or politics, and is an example of exactly what to my mind psychoanalysis should not attempt.

International Journal of Psycho-analysis Volume 67, Part 3, 1986

Primal Repression: Clinical and Theoretical Aspects

Warren Kinston and Jonathan Cohen

Primal repression, long an obscure and unusable concept, has been given a precise place in a recent reworking of the theory of repression (Cohen & Kinston 1984); and this paper specifically examines its properties and presentation. Primal repression refers to an absence of psychic structure which can be made good in the process of emotional growth. It is a part of the mind where trauma persists; and it has a close connexion to the unrepressed unconscious. Direct emergence of primal repression is a threat to life and its activation is therefore risky. During psychoanalysis, primal repression is normally avoided by object-narcissism buttressed by neurotic defences, but it may be reached and worked with in the presence of a non-internalizable valuing and nurturing relationship which we label ‘primary relatedness’. This relation is therefore the interactional context for emotional growth. Numerous clinical examples are provided to demonstrate characteristic features of this region of the mind as seen in psychoanalyses. Vignettes illustrate the experiences of patient and analyst as primary relatedness is established; the consequent re-emergence of traumatic states and unmet needs, often initially in the form of severe physical and psychological deterioration; primitive forms of symbolization in the course of repairing primal repression; and the role of action in emotional growth.



International Review of Psycho-analysis, Volume 13 Part 2, 1986

A Contribution to the Subject of “Psychic Trauma” Based on the Course of a Psychoanalytic Short Therapy

O. Goldschmidt

The paper is based on precise documentation of the analytical short therapy of a patient with a typical traumatic neurosis, extracts from the therapy being presented. The typical case makes it possible to adduce considerations of a theoretical, clinical and therapeutic nature whereby traumatic neurosis can be distinguished from other disturbances - in particular, psychoneurosis. Such considerations are important because pure forms of psychoneuroses and traumatic neuroses are much rarer than transitional forms. In so far as it is possible to show that a typical traumatic neurosis calls for a therapeutic procedure which differs in some respects from that applicable in psychoneurosis, this may have consequences for the handling of traumatic inclusions in patients with predominantly psychoneurotic problems, as well as in other disturbances, such as borderline personality disturbances.

1. British Journal of Medical Psychology, Volume 59, Part 1, March 1986

The Psychotherapy of Mania

Roberto Mester

Focal dynamic psychotherapy with acute manic patients has been a neglected treatment modality. In young adults with sound premorbid personalities and well-developed ambition systems, focal dynamic psychotherapy is useful in the manic stage; it shortens the process of elaboration of major conflicts related to self-image and self-ideal. Three young Israeli soldiers' case material is discussed in whom, due to different growth constellations, the hope to serve in the army in specific capacities had been a central motivating and consolidating factor in their personality development. Their confrontation with the realities and frustrations of military life caused them to react with a manic syndrome which brought them to treatment. Therapeutic insight led to the reshaping of their ambition to a more adaptive level.



2. British Journal of Medical Psychology, Volume 59, Part 1, March 1986

Oedipal Determinants in Differential Outcome of Bereavement

Harwant S. Gill

According to psychoanalytic theory, a bereaved individual's prior relationship with the lost person affects his vulnerability to bereavement. Freud attributed the vulnerability to the intensity of ambivalence, and Fenichel saw Oedipal rivalry as one example of that ambivalence. It is argued that, after the death of a parent, reality testing, crucial to the resolution of the Oedipus complex, is disrupted differently for children of the same sex, from those of the opposite %ex. Based on Freud's and Fenichel's clinical observations, the effects of disrupted reality testing were transformed into a testable hypothesis. The predictions were validated by testing them against the data supplied by patients before they had any professional contact, when two-thirds of bereaved psychotherapy patients exhibited different effects when the deceased parent was of the same sex, from when he/she was of the opposite sex. A majority of the same-sex children develop an unconsciouse sense of guilt, which blocks their expression of Oedipal attitudes towards both parents and which attacks their capacity to function adequately at work, and in their sex-linked roles; while the opposite-sex children maintain their preference for the dead parent, aversion to the alive one, and have idealized expectations of their lovers or spouses.

Melanie Klein by Phyllis Grosskurth. Published by Hodder and Stoughton; 1986; £19.95.

Nini Ettlinger

Nini Ettlinger

Nini Ettlinger  

Had you or I met Frau Klein when early in the century, a young mother of three with little higher education, she was seriously adrift, trapped in the meshes of a severe depressive neurosis, entangled with a bossy mother rather aptly called Libussa, would we have predicted that here was embodied greatness? For years she projected her astonishing creativity into her brother Emanuel, an itinerant artiste manque, who died of tuberculosis in Genoa when she was twenty, just four years before her marriage which would later be dissolved.

A sister whom she dearly loved had died when Melanie was four. Her father died when she was eighteen, Libussa when she was thirty-two, when her youngest son was four months old. It seems that this holocaust precipitated Mrs Klein, by way of discovering Freud's book on Dreams with a sense of deep excitement, into analysis with Ferenczi. So began her love affair with Psychoanalysis.

Antisemitism drove her from Budapest to Berlin into the orbit of Abraham, who became her second analyst for just over a year before he died at the height of his influence. Had you or I met her in Berlin during those post-war years when her couch-sister, Alexis Strachey, was nearly driven round the bend by Die Klein, that chatterbox, even at the Opera, would we have had the intuition to place our confidence in her? Ernest Jones did. He brought her over to England, and even more entrusted his entire family, both his children and his wife, to Klein as an analyst.

Despite her chequered history, as victim of painful circumstances in both her closer and wider world, her undoubted genius lay in her inspired observation of the play of little children. For centuries mothers must have watched their minioffspring collide small lorries, wagons, ox-carts or rickshaws with that familiar furore. But never had it dawned on them as it did on Mrs Klein, consciously at any rate, that they were in fact observing the symbolic collision of a parental intercourse.

A common gambit in the antiques trade is to collect a series of pots made by a little-known factory which has gone out of business, write a book on the subject, and sell the collection at a large profit. In medicine the technique is to define a new entity and write a book on it, which brings us to this volume. It consists of a series of 20 papers on the subject of bisexuality. The first papers attempt to define the condition and measure it with the result that there is a lot of repetition. They all state that the bisexual is different from the hetero and homosexual but this is largely because both the other groups reject him. They are clear that bisexuals are not homosexuals in transition to heterosexuality (indeed most of the clinical examples are in the opposite direction), but sexually flexible individuals. Little reference is made to the fact that most humans can vary their object choice according to the supply of partners, and they consider it is a biological phenomenon that has to be accepted.

One paper, however, by J. M. Carrier emphasises the high prevalence of ‘active’ homosexuals/bisexuals in Mexico, a society which prohibits sex before marriage for women and where marrige is delayed. The same comment could be made about bestiality in rural Turkey. Could it be that Woody Allen was right in suggesting that bisexuality was a way of doubling your chance for a date on a Saturday night!

The rest of the book is largely concerned with the issue of the bisexual in a heterosexual marriage. David Lourea discusses the issues of counselling and there are eight papers giving details of samples, two where the female partner becomes bisexual and six where the male does. Not surprisingly the samples are heavily skewed towards high-income, college-educated volunteers and some of the conclusions can be directly attributed to this bias. Thus Gochros records that 33 women reacted to the disclosure that their husband was bisexual by increased assertiveness and communication skills, the very characteristics which would have caused them to volunteer through newspaper advertisements, and ‘snowballing’ which selects those with the most social contacts.

This book has already received sufficient, merited, good reviews to ensure its place as the vade mecum of the psychologist working with the elderly. It has scholarly reviews of such subjects as the intellectual changes of ageing (few) and of dementia, psychological theories and treatment of depression, assessment, and critical and valid comments on Reality Orientation and Reminiscence therapies, and the role of the psychologist with the elderly. As this book will deservedly become a source book for many professionals working with the elderly is deserves stringent criticism.

As a doctor reviewing a book intended for another profession one could not help be made aware of the gulf that is growing up between psychology and medicine. If a physiotherapist had written a book about arthritis but had failed to distinguish osteoarthritis, autoimmune arthritis, and metabolic arthritis one might regard the book with some suspicion. These authors do refer to the differences in neuropathology of the dementias, but then devote 30 pages to an analysis of the cognitive deficits of dementia as if it was one illness. Depression is also discussed as a unitary phenomenon, bipolar psychosis and mania receiving not a mention. Another notable omission is paraphrenia which is given 18 lines in all and schizophrenia which is ignored. Whilst E.C.T. is not a psychological treatment it has implications for the psychologist but again is not mentioned.

The role of the psychologist in the multidisciplinary team also gives rise to some concern. Assessment and treatment, they say, must be a minor part of the role of the psychologist. ‘We feel it is worth maintaining some individual contact; apart from any benefit to the clients concerned, it helps the psychologist retain credibility, provides refreshment and encourages humility, in their attempts to work at other levels.

Clinical Commentary IV

(A short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the history of the case. The material has been sent “blind” to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention in putting these commentaries side by side is to compare the approaches of the different schools in order to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice).

The Therapist Writes

This forty-year old woman sought help following six months of a severe depression, characterized by agoraphobia, panic attacks, and psychosomatic complaints. For three months she was unable to work at all, and since, has worked part-time. She has been on anti-depressants until very recently. She feels vulnerable and lacking in confidence, and that she approaches life in the wrong way. She says she seeks understanding.

The History

She was raised in a tiny hamlet in the north, in what she describes as a typical working class family. Her mother was the caretaker of the local village hall, and firmly believed that as a girl, her daughter could have no hopes to be anything but a cleaner. Her father was in the Army and absent for the first two years of her life. Her first recollection of him is of his beating her when she was 21/2 years old. This beating continued until she left home at 18. Her father also beat her mother, and she often found herself in-between, trying to protect her.

She had a sister 2 years younger than her, toward whom she was also very protective, who died as a result of a car crash after a gruesome week of gangrene poisoning. Her father has never recovered from the death, for which she blames him, as her sister and her boyfriend were rushing home for the father's strict curfew. She says she has never mourned her sister's death.

School, like home, was an unhappy experience for her. She was a bright child, top of her class in primary school. She won a scholarship to grammar school, but when her father said he couldn't afford the bus fares, she lost interest and just ‘scraped through’ secondary school. At 18 she went to Art College and graduated. Later she took her A levels in the evening. After Art College, she took a variety of jobs and travelled extensively. These travels took her eventually to South Africa where she met and married a man with whom she had a violent relationship.

The main thing that strikes me about this is how the therapist puts herself down. Here is a woman with a very difficult history and a lot of trouble with making relationships, who is responding to therapy in a remarkable way. But the therapist does not take any credit for this, and seems to think she is failing.

224

One of the key things I watch for in therapy is the client taking fire - that is, being affected by the therapy between sessions. In this instance not only did the client think about the therapy - the upsurge of feelings was so strong that she did not even feel able to turn up to the previous meeting. This is a strong indication that the process has really taken root, and after only two months I would consider this a very good achievement.

It seems clear also that the client is beginning to rely on the therapy rather than on the tablets. This again is an indication that the therapist is doing a good job.

It also seems clear that the client has got some of the very important clues about therapy, and is using them herself - the connection between psyche and soma; more than one voice inside herself; the fact that therapy is a long process - and this, too, is evidence of good success on the part of the therapist.

I have often noticed that young therapists very often do not realise how effective they are being. They criticise themselves when they would do better to build on the sound foundations they have put in already. This session seems to be a classic example of this.

The client is good, too. The whole episode about the marriage, and the husband's weird habits, serves at least three purposes. One: it says to the therapist - “Look, I trust you enough to admit that I am thinking about you even when I am not with you.” Two: it says - “I trust you enough to deal with this sensitive and embarrassing material.” Three: it says - “I want to test you by giving you someone else's sexuality; if you treat that properly, I may trust you with something about my own.” This is a very economical use of time by the client, to kill so many birds with one stone.

John Denford

John Denford

John Denford  

This person's complaint suggests: considerable anger which she feels the need to try to contain within herself (her depression); fears that she will lose control of it (panics and agoraphobia); and tends to contain within her body as well by focusing her attention on body parts, their sensations and functions, and experiences her negative feelings there, and her fears about their dangerousness (psychosomatic complaints).

I assume that her anger relates to circumstances and events in her life which she feels are destructive to her (the failure of yet another relationship). They control her. She cannot find any solution which will reverse this state of affairs, so feels helpless and more or less hopeless about changing them. I assume also that the present circumstances which have such disturbing effects do so partly because of their real qualities but also because they contain elements which repeat similar ones in her early life, when she was dependent in fact and unable to influence or control anything. This is why she cannot detach herself psychologically from what is hurtful in the present. Hurtful circumstances and helplessness in face of them are integral elements of her personality.

The initial anger, the depression, the panics and the counter phobic manoeuvres as well as the development of somatic complaints, all represent attempts to grapple with what is wrong, and beginnings of solutions, but are all over-shadowed by a basic conviction that they will not succeed. The repetitious, inert, obsessive quality of her depression and phobias express these wishes to contain and resolve, as well as the conviction of there being no solution, but that it is better to something than nothing.

A rational therapeutic response to this state of affairs would seem to be the offer of a human relationship in which, first, understanding of all these mechanisms could be established, especially through the demonstration of transference responses (the way in which memories of the earlier both hurtful and helpful experiences unconsciously influence and even determine present perceptions, assumptions, and expectations). Second, by establishing clear understanding of negative and destructive possibilities in the relationship, wholly or partly to circumvent them to establish an effective therapeutic alliance or enough trust; third, to allow the development and exploitation of a relationship in which psychological solutions to her repetitive problems (including detachment from them) can be developed. Such a therapeutic relationship and its achievements can be incorporated as significant and persistent new elements in the patient's (and therapist's) personality. Subsequent use of such elements might produce in turn secondary effects in the patient's life, with both people and things, which could further reinforce their existence as convincing parts of her personality, and have cumulative, integrative effects throughout the rest of her life.

This book has two very clear aims; firstly, to present the most relevant up-to date data and factual evidence on women's mental health problems, causes and treatment; and secondly, to present recommended changes and alternatives for improving prevention and treatment of women's mental health problems. Its statement of intent is forthright and sets the scene for an aggressive discourse on a very pertinent feminist issue.

The book is divided into five sections, each of which begins with a concise well-referenced summary of the topic covered by the section followed by articles of opinion, theory or case history, and in three sections ending with a summary of practical comments as to how solutions might be found.

In Section One the issue of whether there is over-representation of women among the mentally ill is discussed. Psychoanalytic and biological/genetic explanations of why this might be so are rejected in favour of a combined model of external stress, internal psychological change and individual vulnerability. The authors are not attempting to equalise sex differences but by taking a sociocultural approach which emphasises demographic and stress factors in women's environment they are aiming to change the perspective, from which mental health problems may be viewed. In this section the prevalent disorders of women are identified as depression, agoraphobia, psychosomatic disorders in the genital/ reproductive tract, marital and family problems and eating disorders. Four factors affecting women's health are identified which form a recurrent theme throughout each section of the book: the socialisation process of women, the social status of women, discrimination against women and the biases that support inequality.

In the second section of the book the case for sexist treatment in the mental health system is examined. The five contributors here vary from a social psychology teacher to an ‘ex-psychiatric inmate, and very angry woman’. There is sexual bias in clinical judgement due to erroneous stereotyping and there is sexual exploitation by therapists, both subtle and blatant. The criteria for admission of women as inpatients is looser but so is the organisation of post-hospitalisation facilities.

Angela Molnos  

While outside the nordic summer staged a rapidly changing mixture of shower bursts, sunshine and crystalline skies, the First European Symposium on Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy took off the ground on the premises of the University of Copenhagen in a spirit of friendliness and impartial objectivity. One of the most memorable features of this symposium was the genuine mutual interest with which participants scrutinised each other's work. There was no cult of personalities, present or absent. Instead credit was given to all those who have contributed to the development of brief psychotherapy. The few opening words by the President, Jytte Vestergaard-Bogind, said it in a nutshell. With great simplicity she declared that the aim of the symposium was ‘to bring together different initiatives in short-term dynamic psychotherapy’.

The 120 participants represented a wide range of centres of excellence dedicated to clinical work, psychotherapy research and training. The bulk of the participants came from Norway, Sweden and, of course, Denmark. The host country contributed mainly with the imaginative multidisciplinary approach developed at Montebello, a model psychotherapy hospital in Helsingor. Their programme of shortterm inpatient treatment of neurotics, with ongoing psychotherapy training for all interested staff, unfolded through several free papers and video-presentations.

Individual participants came from Finland, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Switzerland, the United States and Yugoslavia. The transcultural nature of the gathering - or perhaps of psychotherapy as a whole profession - acquired a poignant dimension as one kept on meeting more and more participants who were born in a country other than the one their nametag purported to be the case. It was nevertheless strange that the only person from the UK should be someone born in Hungary, namely myself … The absence of more participants from outside Scandinavia, especially from France, the German-speaking countries, Italy, Spain and the UK was noted with great regret and remains largely inexplicable.

(Shakespeare)

It is remarkable that more than half a century elapsed before the subject of The ‘Applicability of Psychoanalytic Treatment at an Advanced Age’ raised by Abraham (1919) was re-opened by King (1974). Certainly Freud (1904, 1905) had given his reasons for considering ‘old people are no longer educable’, but Sandler (1978) has suggested that his view was coloured by personal anxieties and preoccupations about ageing. So it seems possible that the quotation may account for the lapse of time between Abraham and King.

Since King wrote ‘Notes on the Psychoanalysis of Older Patients’ (1974) a number of analysts have found that some older people can respond to this form of treatment.

Psychotherapy for those in later life is still unusual, and as far as I know it is only Bella and Small (1978) who suggest that brief psychotherapy may be of particular use to those in later life. Brief psychotherapy has been developed by Malan (1976) and colleagues, and criteria have been worked out by extensive clinical and research experience. The two triangle technique described by Malan (1979) has been extended by Molnos (1984) and I have found it a most useful conceptual framework. I first attempted brief psychotherapy with an older patient when I worked with an aged man suffering from unresolved grief (Hunter 1981). It was this experience which led me to attempt it again with the patient who forms the subject of this paper.

I shall refer to the patient as Mary. She was sixty-eight and was referred as suffering from unresolved grief. There is extensive literature on the subject of grief but it is Tyson's (1983) paper which is particularly relevant to my work. He draws attention to the need to understand, from a developmental perspective, the effect of object loss on the narcissistic equilibrium of the bereaved and considers omnipotence, self-constancy and self-esteem the special components of this equilibrium. The other papers of special relevance are Freud's, ‘Jokes and their Relation to the Unconscious’ (1905) and ‘Humour’ (1927), and Winnicott's ‘The Capacity to be Alone’ (1958) and ‘The Use of an Object and Relating through Identification’ (1971).

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

In this issue we are continuing with a policy of generating continuing contributions on certain issues. In the last issue we started a series of material on the importance of infant observation, with the previously unpublished paper of Esther Bick. And in this issue we have a ‘Clinical Commentary’ using some material from a session of an infant observation. Infant observation is a training and research method that was pioneered by Esther Bick in the 1950's, first of all in the training of child psychotherapists, and then in the training of adult psychoanalysts in Britain. It is now a method that is adopted in an increasing number of psychotherapy trainings. The observer goes to the family home once a week and spends an hour with the baby and mother, forming a relationship that is not professional or therapeutic. Set up as an opportunity for the advantage of the observer, it frequently acts as an important support for the mother herself as a side-effect. For those psychotherapies that accept the importance of early influences in the development of the personality, direct observation of infants in their primary relationships with their mothers is clearly of very great value. At the same time of course the fundamental emotional experience of witnessing this growing relationship is enormously enhancing for the trainee in his own development and for all trainees in their own therapy. The Clinical Commentary shows the different frameworks within which it is possible to consider the infant's earliest relationship.

In future issues we will be publishing a short series of papers on infant observation during the first year of life. And that will commence in the next issue. The forty years of psychoanalysis were concerned with working out childhood developmental processes from the pathology of adults. This was a productive activity. There were practical advantages to do it that way; however, on the face of it, a more rational procedure would seem possible. And around 1920 child psychoanalysis was developed as a way of confirming the discoveries with adult patients. Interestingly what happened was that the results of child psychoanalysis were to provide evidence of reconstruction of earlier developmental history - in infancy. And this has had a very profound impact on the practice of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. But, another forty years on, the next step was to find a way of looking directly at infantile development. And this too is beginning to have an impact on the practice of child and adult psychotherapy and psychoanalysis. In this issue we have a paper by Dorothy Judd in which she describes the course of a child psychotherapy, employing concepts that come out of Bick's descriptions of early infantile relationships.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

In this issue of the Journal we are very pleased to be able to publish a littleknown and unpublished paper by Esther Bick. She died in July 1983, leaving very little published evidence of her work in psychoanalysis. In spite of this she has left behind a powerful influence on those she trained and worked with. The publication in the Journal of a further paper brings her ideas to many more people, albeit in a very much more indirect way.

She was a devoted supporter and also a personal friend of Melanie Klein. If Freud discovered the child in his adult patients, Klein had gone back to look at the child and discovered the infant there. Esther Bick continued in this direction by working directly with infants. To do this she developed the infant observation technique, which is now a familiar feature of many psychotherapeutic trainings in this country. She reported this in a paper in 1964. With the new technique, she began to discover, with her students, new aspects of the psychology of infancy. She conceptualised this as the infant's experience of his own skin. The skin is not just a very important organ for perception in the new-born, but through its sensations, the skin comes to acquire the experience of an organ actually holding him together (or at times failing to do so and letting him fall apart). This view of the early experiencing of the infant is clearly parallel with the ideas being developed at the time by Bion (containing) and Winnicott (holding). However Esther Bick always distinguished her views from both Bion and Winnicott since, I think, she felt that the experience of holding was initially a sense of being held together, in a purely bodily way. And the eventual psychological phenomenon of ‘holding’ derived from a precursor in the bodily sensations. Thus she was in the tradition of Freud's comment that the ego was firstly a body-ego, and she gained access back to very primitive states of undifferentiation between mind and body. These research results of the new technique were published in 1968, and thereafter, as far as I know, she published nothing. However at this time she was working with Donald Meltzer whose interest had turned to autistic children. Understanding of the mind of the autistic child seemed to entail a similar suspension of the idea of a mind, since what psychological events that could be described appeared to happen without a sense of a mental place in which they were happening. Mrs. Bick's ideas fitted well with Dr. Meltzer's own conceptualisations and he repeatedly refers to Mrs. Bick's work. Between them they created the concept of adhesion or adhesive identification, a development elegantly described by Dr. Meltzer in a lecture published in 1975. At about the same time (the mid-seventies) Mrs. Bick also wrote the present paper, in which she takes her results beyond mere research and shows how the discovery of the vicissitudes of this moment when an infant emerges into a mental being is important in clinical practice with children and adults.

Uncertainty is the very condition to impel Man to unfold his powers.

(Erich Fromm, Man for Himself, 1947)

Several years ago an intelligent and troubled friend of mine, I shall call her Carol, then in her mid-twenties, was sent to a psychiatrist because of worsening symptoms of depression. She remembers him as a kind, fatherly man who asked her a comprehensive range of questions to survey her symptoms, life and dilemmas. Before she left, he informed her of his view that her pattern of distress would be ‘best treated by psychotherapy’ and that he would make arrangements accordingly. Carol, although a bright and educated young woman, came from a background largely alien to matters psychological and introspective. Her parents, pragmatic Northerners from an industrial city, represented a culture and way of thinking very different from the psychodynamically sophisticated psychiatrist she encountered; she did not know what psychotherapy was and he, perhaps unwittingly, did not explore this gulf between them. It was several weeks before Carol received a standardised letter from the hospital telling her of an appointment with Dr. L., a psychotherapist, in four months' time.

By the time Carol went to see Dr. L. her most troublesome depressive symptoms had largely subsided, perhaps due to medication she had been prescribed. She was however left with a churning, ineffable chaos inside her which became heightened on the day of her appointment; the fantasy of her imminent meeting with Dr. L. produced an added, tense composite of hope and fear. A long period of waiting in a neon-lit and threadbare waiting area preceded the appearance of Dr. L. ‘Miss Jackson? I am Doctor L. Will you follow me please,’ was Dr. L's sparse greeting. His voice seemed uncompromisingly dry and neutral, Carol thought, as she was led along a corridor and into a small bare room in which there were two easy chairs. Dr. L. closed the door behind them and silently gestured to one of the chairs as he sat down himself. A period of silence followed which, for Carol, was unexpected and increasingly uneasy. Her previous encounters with her own doctor and the psychiatrist had been in some ways embarrassing and difficult, but reassuringly structured by the initiative they took in asking questions and offering explanations and suggestions of various kinds; at those times she had felt encouraged by the elementary support and interest shown to her. [[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy and the Public Domain

Barry Richards

Barry Richards

London E15 211

Barry Richards  

This paper is an attempt to raise some questions about the relationship of psychotherapy, or rather of psychotherapists, to the ‘public domain’, that is to politics in the broadest sense of the whole field of debate, conflict and decision concerning social ends and choices, from residents' associations to foreign policy. Before embarking on this discussion about psychotherapists though it is necessary to sketch out something of the more general conceptual field within which these questions are to be raised.

The existence of a ‘public domain’ is premissed upon the separation of ‘public’ and ‘private’. That separation deeply structures our life-space; in some form it is probably to be found in all human societies (Elshtain 1981). Its present form seems to be in large part a feature of industrial capitalism and its removal of the sphere of work from that of home. With this split goes the separation of instrumental and worldly relations from affective ties, and of individual workers' outward performances from their inner sense of purpose and value (see for example Zaretsky 1976). These separations are many-sided and complex and their history contentious.

The present significance and value of the public-private distinction are also in contention. A theme of ‘Sixties’ radicalism was that ‘the personal is political’, by which it was usually meant that the distinction was somehow false or superficial. This assertion generated some important insights into the societal meanings of personal distress and its connections with social relations of class, gender and race. It failed though to appreciate the historical depth and moral complexity of the separation and distinctness of the public and private domains.

Another major critique of the public/private divide, one developed particularly within feminism, acknowledges it to be a major social and psychological reality, but sees it as largely pernicious in its effects. From this point of view much social decision-making (especially, for example, defence policy) is seen as being carried on in a dehumanised way, split off from the nurturant sensibilities found only in authentic personal relations.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

The effect of a research programme on the psychotherapeutic relationship while under research raises anxieties in the therapists. Jenny Firth, David Shapiro and Glenys Parry have taken those worries seriously and describe the kinds of problems that the demands of a research programme give rise to. The conclusion that such reality factors as the research imposes, can be dealt with as any other reality factor in the course of a treatment, is in fact reassuring, and suggests that the caution with which most psychotherapists approach research has as much to do with the therapist's phantasies as with the patient's - a seemingly more threatening eventuality. And one which creates the rift between practitioners and researchers. The evidence that research can attend to the extreme sensitivity of the therapeutic encounter is heartening as it must go some way to dispel the anxiety that research inevitably introduces unmanageable artefacts into the treatment, and the expectation that the individuality of each patient and his treatment has in the course of the research to be reduced to a tabulated series of non-individual regularities and conformities.

It is perhaps true also that psychotherapists regard the individuality of each patient as a research task in itself each time a new treatment is started. And every patient is a source of learning for each psychotherapist all through his career. It is one of the essential attractions of psychotherapy, that there are always new challenges to face. Routinization does not set in, in our work. This is why so often the publication of a single case study is warranted. Joan Hunter's application of brief psychotherapy to an elderly person's bereavement, is an unusual challenge. In itself a single case prompts the possibility of a new field of development.

Brief psychotherapy is also commented on by Angela Molnos, whose report on a recent conference, emphasizes the curious ascendency of Davanloo's approach which seems to alternately inspire and horrify.

Margaret Mahler - 1897-1985

Harold Maxwell

Harold Maxwell

Harold Maxwell  

Margaret Mahler died on 2nd October 1985 just a month before the first international symposium on her work to be held outside the United States took place in Paris.

She could be said to be the third of a triumvirate of Austrio-Hungarian Matriarchies all born between 1882 and 1897 who were to become of the greatest significance in the theory of the psychology of child-development leading to particular views and concepts of child and adult psychoanalytic theory and practice.

It is difficult not to suggest that the researches of Margaret Mahler have less significance than those of Anna Freud and Melanie Klein, if one accepts the views of Anne-Marie Sandler in a review of The Psychological Birth of the Human Infant: Symbiosis and Individuation by Mahler, Pine and Bergman (International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 1976 Vol. 57 Part 3 pp. 360-362). Sandler states

It would be no exaggeration to say that this work represents one of the most comprehensive modifications of the psychoanalytic theory of child development since Freud published his Three Essays in 1905. I would venture to suggest that Mahler's views would have been perfectly acceptable to Freud, for they are based on the most careful and essentially psychoanalytic observation of infants and children, normal and abnormal.

Mahler was born in the Hungarian town of Sopron, near the Austrian border some forty miles from Vienna, where she in due course became a doctor, a pediatrician and later an inspired child psychiatrist, psychoanalyst and child analyst. In 1938 the Nazi threat forced her to emigrate first to London, where she had some analysis under Willi Hoffer, and later to the United States.

Later the expression Symbiotic Psychosis was used in those situations where it was clear that the mother-child unit remained as a unit, and the mother was not experienced as a separate object. The illness began, in fact, at a point where this would normally happen, so that the lack of separation was psychically brought about by various bodily disorders of perception. Panics were thought to be typical of the Symbiotic Psychosis; while in the Autistic Psychosis, excitation - both inner and outer - cannot be coped with due to the absence of a tie with mother.

Pamela Hawes and Helle Munro

Helle Munro

Ms Helle Munro, c/o, 19 Fitzjohn's Avenue, London NW3.

Helle Munro  

Nine months after I left the Henderson Hospital my social worker, Ann, refused to see me alone: individual counselling was to stop. Instead she offered, together with a marriage counsellor, to work with both Pete and myself. My jealousy was unbearable, waves of anger, flowed through me. Blame? What had I done wrong? Deep, deep feelings of love. Was that why?. Oh the pain, such a pain, in my tummy. There were no words to explain. I did not know some of these feelings, or where they came from. I remembered similar feelings in my teens, anger directed at my mother; jumbled up emotions that would sweep through my body in quick succession. Violence and self destruction; love; fear of being completely out of control.

I knew that hospitalisation would again only suppress what was wrong. During my teens a hospital cell, ECT and drugs held me.

I had a repeat episode in my mid-twenties. I met Pete when I was seventeen and married him soon after. We had two children and settled down in a new town outside London. I lived in a fantasy of being a perfect mother and wife for five years. Any marital problems were pushed away; after all, in a perfect set-up there is no room for problems. Inevitably this fantasy crashed. It happened when we moved back to London and my younger child started school. My past plagued me to the point that I was again admitted to a mental hospital. My life began to shatter around me. The children went into care, and our marriage was in considerable danger of breaking up. The hospital treated me with drugs and ECT again, and any thoughts or feelings from childhood were once more suppressed.

Commentary by an Independent Psychoanalyst

Patrick Casement

Patrick Casement

Patrick Casement  

When looking at someone else's clinical work I think we should always remind ourselves that we were not there; and the therapist, who was there, was subjected to the impact of the patient's presence and the pressures to speak and to be effective in the session. I therefore wish to regard the following commentary as an exercise in practising with clinical material, to recognise some different ways of responding and the implications of each.

Here we have a young man who finds himself ill prepared for life beyond home and school. Within the home he is described as having been in a mutually supportive relationship with mother, looking after a depressed father. But an alternative model for relating may have been developed through identification with this withdrawn and inaccessible father. The patient has also been deprived of relationships in which a surviving firmness could allow for confrontation and for aggression to be expressed and yet contained, which would have served both communication and relating. These tentative formulations I would hold in abeyance. I would be careful to avoid imposing these upon my understanding of the patient.

Throughout this session the communication seems to oscillate between quick-fire questioning and long pauses. If we use trial identification we can readily sense that the patient would feel put under pressure by the questioning; and the therapist may well have felt under pressure from the silences.

I therefore find myself wondering whether there may be an interplay here between patient and therapist, whereby the therapist is meant to know what the patient is thinking or feeling: a symbiotic mother-transference, perhaps? Alternatively, is the therapist being prodded into becoming the mother ‘who kept things going’ (a role-responsiveness to the patient identified with the withdrawn father)? However, there are insufficient grounds in this session for interpreting either of these possibilities. Instead, we can follow the interaction with these transference possibilities kept passively in mind.

When in the session described above the patient reports that he does not feel ‘plugged in’ and in persecuted ‘for being slow’, he explains how he immediately transforms this particular persecutory anxiety into ‘quite a good experience’, as if he were telling his therapist that he found the tolerance of persecution beyond his capabilities. We also read that the therapist's second question (‘Do you think I am all here’) diverts the patient from another type of anxiety: that of not being emotionally able to get himself to this particular session. Although it is true that the patient may be afraid of letting himself be affected by the therapist, there is little evidence of this at the time the therapist suggests it. There is however evidence that the patient ‘thinks’(?) there is something like a relationship going on, with the therapist ‘maybe’ present and with himself about to arrive. His response to this ambiguous state of affairs is to ‘go blank’, feel ‘weird’, ‘feel nothing’. But both therapist and patient know that he did have an experience when arriving at his session and that something is forcing him to acknowledge an encounter with the therapist - outside and inside.

This experience is rather beautifully described in the dream. In it the idealisation of the persecutory breasts (the beautiful witches) into whom he has projected his ‘twirling’ self and his wistfulness is followed by the experience of feeling ‘drawn in’ (or being drawn into a feeding situation) in a rather seductive, enticing way. The infant in the patient has the experience of being pulled into the session with questions and other gratifications in order to help him establish a feeding relation to the analytic breast. But this does not happen. Instead it becomes eroticised through the manic exhilaration in the dream and the reference to the patient's ‘sexuality’ in the session. It is my impression that it is not ‘homosexuality’ or adult sexuality that is the issue, but infantile sexuality at an oral level that fails in the transference with the subsequent manic flight into idealisation and eroticisation.

This is a political book. It is a compilation of essays that are against capitalism and for the psychology of infancy. They explore social phenomena from a Marxist perspective using a psychoanalytic framework. Some contributors to the book are connected with a recent venture to establish a new psychotherapy journal (known as Free Associations) concerned with the cultural, philosophical and political relevance of the psychotherapies.

The eager use that Marxists have been making recently of psychoanalytic concepts is of some interest to psychotherapists. This book documents the thinking of a young group of Anglo-American radicals whose political leanings derive from the frothy enthusiams of 1968. In May that year Parisian students started a revolution. Curiously it had a strong psychoanalytic flavour, inspired by Herbert Marcuse and Jaques Lacan.

Only after that event did it become apparent to the ordinary Anglo-Saxon world that you didn't have to be a Stalinist to be a Marxist, you didn't even have to like Russia. There seemed to have grown up a brand of Marxism that was specifically West European. For many of us insular English that was almost as bad as being Russian. However the Western forn of Marxism was strongly humanist, and contrasted with the economic determinism of orthodox Soviet communism. And being humanist it took account of human experience, and had for a long time been attempting to digest psychoanalytic views and integrate them -into a radical interpretation of the nature and process of society.

Roberto Mester  

Envy and empathy are both object-related manifestations. The therapist's experience of envy in the course of the therapeutic process is potentially a springboard to the empathic understanding of the patient's immediate psychological state. Steve Kingsbury

Steve Kingsbury

Steve Kingsbury  

Here is a book I have been waiting for: I have read about different therapies before but have never been able, in my mind, to compare them in a way which allowed me to integrate them into a common whole of therapy. This book starts that process.

Chapter 1 is concerned with classifying the various therapeutic arenas and examines how one might make choices between them. The next ten chapters, the core and value of this book, present ten different therapies each written by a leading exponent in their field, covering Freudian, Kleinian and Jungian practice, then personal centred therapy, personal construct therapy, existential therapy, gestalt therapy, transactional analysis, rational emotive therapy and behaviour therapy. Each chapter is written in a common format: historical context and developments in Britain, then theoretical assumptions, and lastly its practice and a case example.

The theoretical assumptions section covers the epistemology of each theory from different viewpoints which include the image of the person, concepts of psychological health and disturbance, and finally acquisition of psychological disturbance and its perpetuation. Each chapter then continues with a section on practice which examines the goals of each particular therapy, the person of the therapist and so the therapeutic style; from this the major therapeutic techniques are discussed and the change process to which they lead. Each chapter then ends with a case example which ties together the approach and displays this in a concise way. In chapter 12 the book moves on to compare two major aspects of the therapists: how various dimensions of personality are explored and therapist activity. Examples of personality dimensions are unconscious/conscious, affective/cognitive and endogenistic/exogenistic. Chapter 13 contains a brief statement by each exponent on their fields limitations, and the last three chapters discuss and present ecological psychotherapy.

It would be possible to discuss this book at great length as it is full of information and chapters 12 and 13, comparing the therapists, could in themselves easily grow into a whole book as the issues they raise are very wide and provoking. So I think I will just keep to what I feel is the real strength of this book; the core ten chapters and the different therapies. The chapters themselves develop each approach well and as they all finish with a case example I was able to form an idea of how the therapy would progress. Then having these ten chapters side by side, in the same room as it were, I could compare in an immediate way the similarities and differences. This is what I really liked: never before have I been able to see all the less ‘orthodox’ therapies together and understand how they fit in with, and relate to, the Freudian, Jungian and Kleinian schools.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

This Journal has achieved a degree of popularity that is extremely heartening to the editorial board, and we have been pleased that the ideas we have had that have got as far as reaching the printed word have been so well appreciated. It is not true that everything about the Journal is positively appreciated by everybody who sees it, as witnessed by the two letters at the end of this issue. So, it may be important, for a Journal that aiming to make a small contribution to the integration of the world of psychotherapy, to recognise that there is a very large field of professional activity and practice involving many many people who do not identify with the world of analytical psychotherapy. It has been the assumption of this Journal that the psychoanalytical form of therapy was the first real psychotherapy and remains the core element in psychotherapy today.

However, psychoanalytic theory is not the only framework for thinking about our work, yet it is the only framework that derives from the study of human beings. Psychological learning theory, towards which most non-analytic psychotherapists turn for their conceptual framework, derives from the study of dogs and rats. In my view the animal species giving rise to a psychological theory is of considerable importance, but it is not the only difference we should take note of. The humanism of psychoanalysis, bearing on the subjectivity of the person and the intersubjectivity of his world, takes analytical psychotherapy dangerously, and excitingly, apart from and probably beyond the world of objective science, as I have noted before in these Editorials. Psychological learning theory, in contrast, remains rooted in the deterministic (non-humanistic) tradition of the objective physical sciences; and in a major sense could be unfortunately allied with the medical and pharmacological approach. Such a contrast between the two conceptual frameworks (subjective and objective) may in fact attract quite convincing judgements of value. Yet the subjective/objective contrast in these approaches to the human mind/brain is in some sense invalid since both mind and brain are inter-related, even if no-one knows how. It may indeed fall to psychotherapists to be the bewildered explorers who stumbled towards the proper understanding of the mind/brain problem - rather than the philosophers who by tradition take it on themselves as their special field of operation. We need more correspondents willing to jump in with opinions upon the great divide in our profession.

Alan Lidmila  

The philosophers have only interpreted the world in different ways; the point is to change it.

(Bottomore & Rubel 1961)

If we substitute psychotherapy or psychoanalysis for philosophy is this an adequate summary of the therapeutic project or is there, as the writers under review suggest, a viable alternative?

The above volumes have much in common and share an infrastructure on various levels. As well as representing attempts to explore the vexed relationship between the psychological and the political world as experienced and as theorised, the writer of one book is also the editor of a series (Critical Texts in Social Work and the Welfare State, General Editor Peter Leonard) of which The Politics of Mental Health is a companion work. Both books share one basic assumption, namely the necessity for transforming social relations for all not merely those who may be suffering more obviously. In order for change to take place it is equally necessary to replace bourgeois theory in any given discipline area with a critical social theory that may in turn inform and guide a practice (in social work, psychology or psychiatry and any related endeavour) in a truly humane and ‘progressive’ direction. In Leonard's terms the central issue of how individuals are constructed under certain historical conditions is a ‘problem of being unable to produce a biographical account of a specific individual from within Marxist categories’ (Leonard 1985, p. 5). He notes that this problem has either been avoided (as in those models consigned to the dustbin of bourgeois psychology) or has been faced unsuccessfully (as in Sartre's union of materialism and existentialism).

These particular statements of critical social theory deserve some sort of full and critical exposition but before attempting this I should perhaps explain why I think this approach to psychotherapy and allied trades demands consideration.

Firstly, the omnipotent desire to achieve a full and complete, a ‘totalised’ understanding of the world has a long and honourable tradition (Laing & Cooper 1965).

Commentary by an Analyst of the Independent Group

A. Brafman

A. Brafman

A. Brafman  

One isolated report of a Baby Observation is like a snapshot which creates a very different impression from that of a series of photographs or of a film. The one report captures images without revealing what preceded them so it is impossible to know if a particular event or sequence occurs for the first and only time or whether it is part of a recurring pattern. The reader can only fall back on his own preconceptions of what is described. This is indeed the premise guiding the present exercise, where several analysts give their interpretations of the report submitted. But our analyses will not influence the observer, let alone the members of the family observed.

The relationship between infant and parents follows quite a different model. The infant's movements and sounds can be perceived, but we cannot know the thoughts, feelings, perceptions, fantasies that accompany those overt manifestations of the infant's contact with the world around him. The parents are continuously interpreting the baby's actions and they do this on the basis of their preconceptions and of their capacity to perceive, interpret and respond to the baby's reaction to each of their interventions. As infant and parents continue their life together, we have a cycle of interactions, where each of them influences the other. If the infant cannot be influenced by the parents or if one or both parents cannot be influenced by the infant, we have a pathological situation. In the normal course of events each of the family members leads the other to repeated adaptations that eventually characterise them as individuals in that particular life context, and together as a family at that point in time of their development.

Setting out to observe the development of a baby in his family, we have to define the theoretical framework dictating our approach and governing the interpretation of our findings, since this will greatly influence the focus of the observations. ‘Baby observation’ as a discipline which is part of psychoanalytic training has traditionally taken the baby as the main focus, but the role of the parents in the life of the infant and child is subject to different conceptualisations. We can find examples of the two main models in the present report.

The background provides us with an outline of Jimmy's human environment and the family's living conditions. We are told that Jimmy, a first child, was delivered some two weeks early by Caesarian section, though we are not told why this intervention was considered necessary. This text by Aaron Beck and his colleagues is a comprehensive and readable volume which is the first book of its kind devoted to an understanding of the theory and practice of cognitive therapy in relation to anxiety. It should be stressed at the outset of this review that the book is based on the ideas and clinical experiences of Beck and his colleagues in developing their particular view of cognitive therapy. It is not a text which draws particularly upon the observations of other cognitive therapists (e.g. Donald Meichenbaum) and does not attempt to develop an overview of a variety of cognitive approaches. Essentially this book is an outgrowth of the work of Beck and his co-therapists and researchers at the Centres for Cognitive Therapy in Philadelphia and California.

It is now well accepted that Aaron Beck was the major proponent in developing a cognitive understanding of the treatment of Depression. His clinical expertise and strategies for intervention with Depression has received some considerable research evaluation and there is an accepted school of therapists who focus on using concepts developed by Beck to help in the treatment of Depression. For those therapists familiar with is work on Depression this present text on Anxiety will be a welcome adjunct to their therapeutic arsenal. In particular since it is common clinical practice to meet patients who present with combinations of problems of a Depressive/Anxious nature then this present volume is especially welcome.

The authors set themselves two major tasks. The first is to attempt to explain the nature of anxiety by understanding it from a cognitive perspective. This section of the book is written by Aaron Beck and draws upon a variety of research and theoretical views on anxiety to explain the concept in cognitive terms. The second task is to provide guidelines for the treatment of the condition. This section is written by Dr. Emery and gives an overview of strategies used in the alleviation of anxiety disorders.

Adolescent Loneliness, Solitude and Psychotherapy

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Barnstaple, Devon

Jeremy Holmes  

Loneliness, a lack, and solitude, a self-sufficiency, are distinguished. Winnicott's concept of the capacity-to-be-alone is described as the basis of solitude. A child who is watched over non-intrusively by a good-enough mother acquires the foundations of solitude in later life. Where the capacity to be alone has not developed adolescent breakdown may occur. The lonely adolescent encounters bodily phantasies which he may be unable to tolerate. Loneliness is then avoided by clinging or isolation. In psychotherapy the importance of these adolescent experiences is often neglected. Part of the therapist's task is to create a setting in which the patient feels ‘held’ enough to be able to tolerate loneliness and so, eventually, to enjoy solitude.

[[RunningHead]]

Oh Yes You Are! Oh No We're Not!

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley  

I intend this to be my last letter in the David Will versus Oakley, Oakley & Gans series to try and halt its deterioration to a psychoanalytic Punch & Judy show with ‘fantasies’, ‘resistances’ etc. being used as ammunition.

Moved by the tragicomic element in Dr Will's ‘a reply to three antipsychiatrists’, (Will 1986), I would like to make three brief points:

On being called an ‘anti -psychiatrist’:

In the hot summer of 1976 a very disturbed patient of mine was hospitalised. The consultant psychiatrist invited me to a staff meeting where I was meant to make ‘an invaluable contribution to the treatment plan (not entirely surprising given that I was the only person at that time apart from the patient's mother who seemed able to make any sense of his discourse). At the end of the meeting I was told by the consultant that I would be ‘allowed’ to visit the patient once a month for five minutes! When I arrived home I received a phone call from the psychiatric social worker on the ward who was very upset and apologised for the consultant's ‘unfair’ decision. ‘She believes’ he said ‘all mental illness to be of physical origin and does not think that relationships have anything to do with it’. He proceeded to say that he himself was in analysis and found it difficult to be away from his analyst at weekends. A month would be unthinkable. In short, would I like him to beg on my behalf?’ ‘No!’ I said, for when I heard the consultant's decision I was faced with a choice: I could take it either as an insult or a joke. I opted for the latter and decided to see my patient if and when he and I thought it appropriate. Now, if being openly critical of this and many more such illustrations of what one might benignly describe as ‘psychiatric insensitivity’ merits the title ‘antipsychiatrist’, I shall gladly carry it. I do however suspect that Dr Will attached the title to my colleagues and me in order to undermine our argument in the eye of the reader. Although my colleagues and I are not in any way associated with it, there is in fact an international anti-psychiatric movement which in recent years played a significant part in amending the mental health act in this country, as well as practically revolutionising the attitude and legislation vis-a-vis psychiatry in Italy. If this is ‘being trapped in a cul-de-sac’, so be it.

The Metaphor of Twinship in Personality Development

Susan Fisher

Susan Fisher

33 Albion Street, London W2 2AX

Susan Fisher  

To develop one's own separate identity and sense of personal authority is a particularly difficult task within a twinship relationship. Twinship creates the additional obstacle of separating from a need-satisfying sibling before progressing to the struggle for separation from mother. This paper examines these difficulties within the metaphor of twinship, linking them to the development of identical twins, object relationships and psychotherapeutic practice. Twinship is discussed as a schizoid phenomenon, with reference to reality, narcissism, relatedness, mirroring, dependency needs, boundaries and space.

Susan Mumford

Susan Mumford

Susan Mumford  

This book constitutes an unusual departure from traditional textbooks on depression. By focusing on phenomenological aspects of depression as experienced by nineteen mental health professionals, including psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, occupational therapists, social workers, nurses and general practitioners, it presents some very interesting insights into and personal accounts of the experience and considers a number of issues generally eschewed among clinicians and mental health professionals. It is not anti-psychiatry and addresses psychotherapists, behavioural psychotherapists and psychiatrists alike. It does however confront us with some of the best and some of the worst aspects of our practices.

Over and above its interest at the sheer descriptive level it leads to a balanced examination of ways of conceptualising depression, of the potential role of depression in personal growth and change, and touches on the controversial issues of the ‘wounded healer’ (Bennet).

The contributors describe a variety of techniques to which they resorted to help them survive their depression and the cognitive therapist will find much useful material here.

The book will be of interest to experienced therapists and clinicians, to those in training and to those trying to cope with depression in themselves, their relatives or indeed their colleagues.

Susan Mumford
