Commentary by a Kleinian Analyst

Edna O'Shaughnessy

Edna O'Shaughnessy

Edna O'Shaughnessy  

I understand I am asked as a Kleinian psychoanalyst to comment on this observation of an infant and his mother. I have selected one or two features (others could have been chosen) and I hope something of my approach can be seen from my remarks. I have not seen the comments of the others.

In the observation reported in detail mother tells the observer that her father died while she was pregnant, and with an ironic apprehension which seems to cover a serious degree of anxiety, she anticipates having to feed her baby and also having to visit her own mother for the weekend. The observer then describes how the wakened baby first greets him with a smile and then greets mother with more than a smile: Jimmy extends both arms to her. This begins a fascinating sequence in the observation, Jimmy's complex, differentiated movements of his arms, which bear, I think, an intriguing relation to how mother has always held him in her arms: she always holds Jimmy with her left arm around him close to her body while feeding him from a bottle in her right hand. The observer describes how after she picked up Jimmy, as soon as his hands were free of the sleeping bag ‘they came together on his chest, the left hand round the right one’. This is Jimmy's duplication of the very way mother holds him round with her left hand and it could be understood as Jimmy's unconscious identification with his holding mother.

The Impact of Research on the Practice of Psychotherapy

Jenny Firth , David Shapiro and Glenys Parry

Glenys Parry

Sheffield, S10 2TN

Glenys Parry  

Psychotherapists may avoid clinical research partly because they perceive much of it to have little relevance to practice and partly because they feel that any methodologically sound research will produce deleterious effects upon the process and outcome of therapy. This paper describes a research project designed to overcome some of the problems involved. It focusses in particular upon the research procedures which affect, for better or for worse, the process and outcome of the therapy. The issues raised by aspects of research such as assessments, tape recordings, and strict time-limits, are discussed using clients' comments and therapists' experiences. It is concluded that tackling the issues as they arise in therapy, rather than denying them, can often enhance the therapy and obviate any negative overall effects.

Selling Dynamic Brief Psychotherapy and Teaching the Patient: Reflections on a Symposium

Angela Molnos

Angela Molnos

15 Elm Lodge, River Gardens, 75 Stevenage Road, London SW6 6NZ

Angela Molnos  

I was sitting on a bench in a picturesque Swiss spa close to the Austrian border. Water was trickling from a fountain. All around were red roses and glorious mountain peaks glittered in the summer sunshine. My mind would not stay with the peaceful scenery, but it took me back to the top of a nearby gorge where I had spent the last few days. Centuries ago that daunting and remote spot was visited by the famous doctor Theophrast von Hohenheim, called Paracelsus, who wrote about the healing power of its waters. There in the old cloister of Bad Pfafers, now restored to be used for conferences, an unforgettable Davanloo-Malan symposium was held. For three days two hundred participants had been gazing at video pictures of patients and the therapist interacting on a large screen at the end of the long and narrow main hall. The comments given by the presenters on each case were brief and to the point. It was an impressive show. Some of those who had not seen Davanloo's work before found in disconcerting. Those of us who have already battled with the technique were only intent on grasping it better; we needed no further convincing.

Malan had declared himself sceptical when he first saw Davanloo's technique. The latter elaborated the point. According to him, not once but for several years, in conference after conference, Malan and other psychoanalysts viciously attacked him contesting his method. This was recounted in a jovial atmosphere in the second half of the symposium. By that time 15 to 20 out of 200 participants had left the meeting in silent protest. They had found little chance to vent their discontent and virtually no opportunity to participate. Having come mainly to listen to Malan, whose books they had read and whose approach to dynamic brief psychotherapy they had learned, they felt painfully let down. Malan now is completely convinced that Davanloo's technique is more effective than his own, which he has described in his books. The main difference in approach is that, following the traditional path, Malan starts softly. He gently interprets first the defence and the anxiety, and only afterwards tightens his grip to get to the hidden feeling: velvet glove covering the iron fist. On the whole he leaves more space for the patient and is less active than Davanloo. The latter starts with iron gloves against the resistance. His firm healing hand, his warmth and compassion become manifest after the patient has given up his defences.

Omnipotence

David Smith

David Smith

London NW1 4NS

David Smith  

Introduction and Historical Note

The following paper consists of a review and critical analysis of three classical accounts of the clinical phenomenon of omnipotence as presented during the early decades of the twentieth century by Sigmund Freud, Karl Abraham and Sandor Ferenczi. Restricting myself to these three theorists will necessarily exclude discussion of more recent contributors to the theory of omnipotence. This is not meant as a denigration of the significance of these contributions, but rather reflects my conviction that many contemporary disagreements within psychoanalysis can be traced back to conflicts of opinion initially articulated during the early history of psychoanalysis.

A survey of the early literature reveals that there was a great deal of interest in the phenomenon of omnipotence during the period immediately preceding World War One. This can be partially attributed to the advent of the theory of narcissism which has been introduced by Isidor Sadger in a discussion of male homosexuality at a meeting of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society on 10 November 1909 and taken up by Freud in the second edition of the Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1910). Because we now take it so much for granted, it is strange to realise that the early analytic theorists were not at first consciously aware of the intimate tie between narcissism and omnipotence. The concept of omnipotence was actually introduced one year before the term ‘narcissism’ emerged in print in a psychoanalytic context. I am referring of course to Freud's discussions of omnipotence in the case of the Rat Man (Freud 1909). It was not until 1912 in ‘Totem and Taboo’ that omnipotence was viewed as a specifically narcissistic phenomenon. After ‘On Narcissism: An Introduction’ (Freud 1914) Freud's explicit references to omnipotence become quite scarce. This is not because he lost interest in the subject but rather because by 1914 he had definitely subsumed omnipotence under the more general clinical heading of narcissism.

Dorothy Judd  

This paper aims to illustrate with clinical material certain basic concepts which emerged in working psychotherapeutically with a ten-year-old girl. These concepts - with particular reference to Klein, Bick and Meltzer - are lack of containment and secondary skin function; adhesive identification and two-dimensionality; projective identification and inner space. Work began with the patient inaccessibly in a two-dimensional state eliciting a frequent counter-transference response of extreme sleepiness. Then at the point at which the therapist was assailed by very powerful physical and emotional sensations in the countertransference, a shift occurred whereby the patient began to use the therapist as an object that could contain some of these projections. A powerful interchange was then under way wherein the patient, with the experience of someone capable of staying with her, developed an awareness of her inner space which could be filled by introjection, as well as that of the therapist which could receive her projections.

The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy by Irvin D. Yalom (3rd edition). Published by Basic Books: New York 1986; 590 pp.; £20.75.

Jeff Roberts

Jeff Roberts

Jeff Roberts  

This is the third and longest edition of a classic text book. Irvin Yalom's Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy was first published in 1970. The two earlier editions were characterised by readability and comprehensiveness. In an extremely reader-friendly fashion Yalom systematically introduces us to a pragmatic interpersonal approach to group psychotherapy which he reviews from all angles. The book is an almost automatic recommendation for the person about to conduct his first group. Almost all that Yalom has to say is supported by his own or other people's research which is listed in a substantial bibliography. Incidentally, in the second edition this appears at the end of each chapter. In this edition it is collected at the end of the book.

As a disciple of Sullivan, Yalom is fundamentally interested in an interpersonal psychotherapy although he has been attracted by other schools of thought including the existential. Psychoanalysis and psychodynamic formulation are not among his strong points so that the book lacks the essential contribution to understanding human motivation and personality structure which is provided by these disciplines. It is this which for me makes this very good book an intermediate rather than advanced text. Yalom's good sense and good humour are ever present; he enables one to think clearly about all kinds of difficult situations, but the management of the most difficult patients and commanding the higher levels of understanding of group processes are not to be found within this volume.

What then of the revisions? What of the chapters remain essentially unchanged with the introduction in some of new clinical examples and the re-writing of certain passages. Chapter five, ‘The therapist's tasks and techniques’, has now been extended and divided into ‘The therapist's basic tasks’ (chapter five) and ‘The therapist working here and now’ (chapter six). In these two chapters Yalom introduces his own ideas about facilitating and commentating on the group process in the therapeutic interests of the individual group members.

The Preserved Nipple Closeness and Distance in the Mothering of a Baby

Christoph Hering

Christoph Hering

63 Roderick Road, London NW3

Christoph Hering  

I first met Mrs Brown some time before the birth of her baby Lucy. During this meeting quite powerful anxieties were expressed by her and already at that time I wondered how these might influence the relationship with her baby.

Mainly three points particularily attracted my attention: (a) Mrs Brown said she did not enjoy being pregnant at all and that she found herself ugly and unattractive; (b) she said that she did not want to breast-feed the baby because she had not enjoyed it with her first child six years ago; and (c) she told me that if the baby were deformed she would under no circumstances keep it, and she added that she did not find babies beautiful.

In fact, at the time of writing, Lucy is ten months old and presents herself as a big and healthy baby girl. Any connection between her present state and mother's early anxieties is not an obvious one. Even during the whole period of my observations Lucy appeared to be a very cheerful and quite contented baby who is neither easily frustrated nor upset. She was never severely ill and showed amazing patience and tolerance in bearing the discomforts of the usual physical complaints such as colds, rashes, bruises and teething. In relation to emotionally difficult situations she struck me as a very forgiving baby who rarely lost her good humour. Today she comes across as an alert, responsive, curious and quite boisterous child who can at times express her likes and dislikes in a forceful way.

However, in the light of the anxieties mother had shared with me before Lucy's birth, certain aspects of my observations became particularly significant and alerted me to what I came to consider a highly conflictual and complex relationship between the baby and her parental environment. It is my understanding that a ‘compromise’ had to be achieved and that it was negotiated around mother's anxieties. In this paper I try to elucidate this ‘compromise’ and to show how it set the scene for a very particular pattern, of relationship. (But before I go into the details of my observations I would like to mention that the difficulties I will be focusing on represent only a small part of the available material. And although, taken in isolation, they may give grounds for worries about and criticism of her parenting, my. overall experience with this family was that these limitations were counterbalanced by a capacity in many other areas of ‘good enough’ parenting.)

The Outcome of Maritally Focused Psychotherapy Offered as a Possible Model for Marital Psychotherapy Outcome Studies

Frederick Balfour , Christopher Clulow and Barbara Dearnley

Barbara Dearnley

Psycho-Analyst and Associate Member, Institute of Marital Studies, Senior Clinical Psychologist, Tavistock Clinic

Deputy Chairman, Institute of Marital Studies and Tavistock Institute of Medical Psychology

Senior Marital Psychotherapist, Institute of Marital Studies and Tavistock Institute of Medical Psychology

Barbara Dearnley  

A model for describing and judging change in a couple relationship is set out, drawing on a follow-up method established at the Tavistock Clinic for the assessment of change in individual patients. We present the follow-up work done with the couple in the chronological order in which it occurred.

Our aim is to show how a psychodynamic formulation of a relationship can be made by using the concept of the shared unconscious phantasy as a factor which describes and justifies treating separate individuals as part of a single system. We suggest that such a framework provides an economic method of formulating a base from which to assess change.

[[RunningHead]]

Coherency and its Disruption in the Development of the Self

Malcolm Pines

Malcolm Pines

London NW3.

Malcolm Pines  

My thesis is that the concept of coherency is fundamental to understanding human psychic development and therefore to the psychodynamic therapies. Basic principles are frequently so taken for granted that we become aware of them through their absence rather than through their presence. The concept of coherency, using this term to represent the meaningful organisation of parts that make a whole, underlies such concepts as identity, integration and unification, all important aspects of personality development. In the study of infant-parental interaction coherency is beginning to be seen as a significant feature. In the psychodynamic process we are engaged in the effort to make meaningful the organisation of therapist and patient, of groups both small and large. Thus in psychoanalysis we try to make sense, to uncover and discover underlying meanings in the analytic discourse, thereby raising what might appear to be incoherent communication to the level of coherency. The more disturbed the patient, the more his utterances become incomprehensible and incoherent; and the more we have to seek in ourselves for the means to make sense to ourselves of what is being said - or left unsaid - thereby to find coherency through our understanding and to make an offer of this to the patient. Advances in the understanding of the more seriously disturbed patient, the borderline and psychotic, come from deeper insights into processes of disorganisation of thought and speech into incoherency, and through a deeper understanding of our own counter-transferential responses.

This issue of coherency is not often addressed directly in the psychoanalytic literature. The exceptions to this, Freud himself and Hans Loewald, will be discussed later. However this issue has been addressed recently by Stephen Marcus in his study of Freud's Case Histories (1984):

Freud addresses parts of experience through creating structures in written language that purport to represent, analyse and make sustained coherence out of these experiences by means of their translation or transposition into such construction of exposition, narrative, analysis or argument as he finds appropriate.

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon  

Kohut's exploration of narcissistic phenomena has had enormous impact on psychoanalytic thinking in the USA. Controversial though ‘Self Psychology’ is, it has stimulated creative debate and a rethinking of many basic assumptions regarding development, the origins of pathology and the mode of action of psychoanalysis. Kohut's influence in Britain, by comparison, is almost negligible. Perhaps this is partly because Kohut - who died in 1981 - was writing against a background of classical analysis, Freudian and ego-psychological, which is rather different to that prevailing in Britain. Here psychoanalytic development has been structured around the contributions of Melanie Klein - either pro-Klein and developing her ideas, or in reaction against Klein. Thus to be meaningful in a British context Kohut's work must be related to Klein. The purpose of this review is to provide a critical evaluation of Kohut's rethinking of narcissism bearing in mind concepts more familiar in Britain. A second brief paper (in this issue) compares more specifically Kohut's ideas to those of Klein and Bion.

The connotations are likely to be that the person is egocentric, grandiose and lacking in empathy for others (e.g. Kernberg 1975). Kernberg, whose formulations are often juxtaposed to those of Kohut, similarly takes an essentially Kleinian view.

N. Dryden  

Dear Dr. Hinshelwood

I write to express my concern about the title of The British Journal of Psychotherapy which you edit. Although at the beginning of the journal's mission statement it is clear that the journal is not “aligned with any one psychotherapy …”, the journal's emphasis is on “clinically oriented papers which concern the practice of analytical psychotherapy”. Indeed at the beginning of your recent editorial you say that “The Policy of the Journal is to provide as wide a spread of interesting material on psycho-analytical psychotherapy as possible”. Vol. 2 (2).

My concern is that the title of your journal leads one to expect a journal that is non-aligned but yet it is clear the focus is very much on psychoanalytic psychotherapy.

As an editor of two international journals in the field of psychotherapy, I am unhappy with the title and believe it creates a false impression of the journal and also possibly of the state of psychotherapy in Britain which is, of course, wider than psychoanalytic psychotherapy as I show in the series I edit for Harper & Row entitled “Psychotherapy in Britain”.

I await your response with interest.

Yours sincerely,

W. Dryden, Ph.D.,

Senior Lecturer in Psychology, Goldsmiths College

(Co-Editor, Journal of Cognitive Psychotherapy; Associate Editor (Europe) International Journal of Eclectic Psychotherapy)

A Note on Kohut and Klein Idealisation, Splitting and Projective Identification

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Gateshead, Tyne & Wear NE9 5BY

Phil Mollon  

Idealisation was considered by Kohut to be an important component of narcissism. In Britain the notion of idealisation is associated most strongly with the theories of Melanie Klein. The following is a brief discussion of possible points of contact as well as major areas of difference between the two approaches.

Melanie Klein (1946) described idealisation, not in the context of narcissism, but as part of an early defensive splitting and idealisation in which, in an effort to deal with overwhelming instinctual forces of life and death, good and bad aspects and experiences of the object are in phantasy kept apart. An idealised object is sought to protect against a persecutory one. Kohut does not explicitly distinguish narcissistic idealisation from idealisation that is a function of splitting of good and bad perceptions of the object. It seems unlikely that what he describes is entirely unrelated to the idealisations described by Klein. One clue is provided by Gedo (1981) who, drawing on Kohut, distinguishes true idealisation from pseudo-idealisation - the latter seeming more obtrusive, insistent or ‘noisy’, perhaps being a response to the breakdown of true idealisation, as in the case of Mr B. What Kohut seems to envisage is an initial quiet idealisation, which in healthy development is optimally disrupted. Gedo remarks:

… typically the omnipotent other is a symbiotic object whose availability and perfection are therefore taken for granted. This is why an idealising transference tends to be silent: insofar as it becomes explicit, it will have an impersonal quality. (p. 127)

Thus the idealisation may focus on the functional capacities of the object rather than the person per se. In the idealising transference it may be the process or technique of analysis that is idealised. This point bears some similarity to Winnicott's notion of the ‘environment mother’ denoting the mother's functions as distinct from the person of the mother.

The gradual disruption of the idealising selfobject relationship in normal development has perhaps some connection with Klein's depressive position - the stage of lessening projection, splitting and idealisation in which the infant feels more separate and has a more integrated and realistic perception of its objects. According to Kohut, if the disruption is traumatic a state of fragmentation occurs - a regression to the fragmented body imago, brooding hypochondria and the emergence of archaic forms of narcissism, such as primitive grandiosity and phantasies of omnipotent objects. This may bear some relation to the splitting and fragmentation described by Klein. One difference is that Klein sees the splitting as an active defensive process whereas Kohut sees fragmentation as a helpless falling apart in response to selfobject failure.

Further Considerations on the Function of the Skin in Early Object Relations

Findings from Infant Observation Integrated into Child and Adult Analysis

Esther Bick

Esther Bick

Esther Bick  

In 1968 I presented a paper built around clinical experiences and infant observations ‘concerned with the primal function of the skin of the baby and of its primal objects in relation to the most primitive binding together of parts of the personality not as yet differentiated from parts of the body’ (Bick 1968). There I described some of the evidence suggesting that in the earliest times the parts of the personality are felt to have no inherent binding force and fall apart unless passively held together, an experience indistinguishable from feeling the body to be held together by the skin. The suggestion was also made that in the event of defective development of this containment function other ‘secondary skin’ devices may arise, in collaboration with particularities of the maternal care, such as muscular or vocal methods. The consequences for personality development were briefly illustrated, with special reference to ego strength, pseudo-independence and tendency to disintegration.

In the present communication I wish to extend those findings and to investigate them in greater depth. The same child, Mary, whose material served originally, will most usefully open the area to investigation if described in somewhat greater detail. She came to me for analysis at the age of three and a half years for reasons of severe general retardation which relentlessly followed on from a difficult birth; the mother had a Caesarean section after a prolonged and futile attempt to deliver her normally. In the very first week she manifested severe clamping on the nipple so that it could hardly be removed from her mouth, and in the second week the mother lost much of her milk. Mary then became a lazy feeder but was always impatient to come to the breast, which she would not surrender until she was eleven months old. She was quite intolerant to separation from the outset, so that mother could never go out in the evenings, all of which was greatly aggravated when she developed eczema at four and a half months of age. Her night-time scratching was so severe, to the point of bleeding, that she had to sleep with her mother, who held her hands as the only method of both restraining and calming her.

Discussion of Esther Bick's Paper ‘Further Considerations on the Function of the Skin in Early Object Relations’

Donald Meltzer

Donald Meltzer

Donald Meltzer  

Esther Bick was a gifted therapist and teacher whose great difficulty in writing has deprived us of a record of the scope of her observations and ideas. The patient described as ‘Mary’ was undoubtedly the most moving, arduous and enlightening clinical experience in her life and most of her richest ideas were derived from that work. But it was the correlation of analytical data with infant-mother observations that fashioned the concepts about which she felt the strongest conviction. While these ideas of skin-containment, second-skin formation, the dead-end, looping, adhesive identification and dimensionality went beyond what Melanie Klein had described with regard to infantile development and psychopathology, Mrs. Bick's approach was completely Kleinian in its preoccupation with object relations and narcissism, with persecutory and depressive anxieties, with modes of defence and types of identification. Despite her professional background in psychology she was less interested in cognitive development as was, for instance, Roger Money-Kyrle, or in thinking processes, like Bion or myself. For this reason she did not follow up the line of inquiry into dimensionality as I was doing in the research group on autism, and later preferred to speak of ‘adhesive identity’ rather than ‘identification’ since the cognitive implications and the impairment of symbol formation did not attract her interest.

I mention these facts in order to introduce an attempt to show the way in which Esther Bick's work, Bion's ideas and my own approach described the same universe of phenomena from different and complementary points of view. I am speaking of work that went on in the period following Melanie Klein's death, in the sixties and early seventies, when Mrs. Bick and I were working very closely together but neither of us had any direct contact with Bion and before Bion's ideas had worked their way into the centre of my own clinical preoccupations. It was, historically, a period in which the enthusiastic exploration of schizophrenia by Kleinian analysts had rather spent itself, for the concept of the paranoid-schizoid position failed to penetrate the mysteries of delusional systems any further than Freud had managed with the Schreber case. Perhaps the paranoid-schizoid position was never achieved by some children or could be lost as an organised state in severe regression. The thesis of minute splitting processes in object relations or narcissistic organisations did not seem to cover the phenomena. Rather it seemed that basic mental functions had been attacked and lost or never developed.

Shame and Envy

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

41 Weston Park, London N8

Joseph Berke  

In this paper I have discussed the nature of shame and its relation to envy. Shame arises from a sudden unwelcome awareness about oneself, while envy is provoked by the painful perception of discrepancies between oneself and another. Both shame and envy aim to eliminate the subsequent tormenting inner tension by rageful, destructive attacks on the real or imagined causes of the torment. However, with shame it is the tension itself which most people recognise as shame, while with envy it is the angry discharge which follows. In fact the model is the same for both which leads to the conclusion that shameful tension is a variation of, as well as a contributor to, envy.

In this, the first of two related papers, the process is examined by which a couple were helped to separate, temporarily and emotionally, through a brief offer of psychodynamic therapy. Mara Sidoli

Mara Sidoli  

[In this section a short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material as published here was sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention in putting these commentaries side by side is to compare the approaches of the different schools in order to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice.]

The Observer Writes

The family live in a poorly-kept house in a rather poor area. However their flat is well decorated and furnished. Although it is often untidy they clearly take an interest in the home and choose the decorations, furnishings etc. with care. The flat consists basically of two large rooms so Jimmy did not have a room to himself. They were trying to look for a larger flat, which they could afford but the smallness of the accommodation seemed to me to reflect the closeness of the relationships between the members of the family.

Jimmy is the first child of young parents, delivered by Caesarean section some two weeks early. There had originally been some doubt about Mother's fertility but she had ‘disproved’ that by becoming pregnant the first month they tried for a baby. She is a plump woman in her early twenties, who greeted me without fuss or self-consciousness when I first met her in the hospital. She was a woman of average intelligence with excellent commonsense and intuitive sensitivity to Jimmy.

Father was present only very occasionally. He was a small man, shorter than Mother, with a working-class background and a grammar-school education. He was very proud of Jimmy and imagined with pride what an active strong boy he would grow up to be. He was extremely courteous to me on the occasions when we met but seemed embarrassed on the one occasion when he was giving Jimmy the bottle.

Jimmy was breast-fed, I think from birth. She would hold him always in the crook of her left arm, his head held closely against her left breast, while she fed with the bottle in her right hand. Mother showed herself to be very sensitive to Jimmy in the early sessions. She was clearly anxious when he became distressed and at times this made her stiff and clumsy. At times she clearly needed support and ‘mothering’ for herself.

'Castration anxiety - which is related to the expectation of the loss of a precious object - is only one aspect of the castration complex. Attention is here drawn to its other side, so far neglected in psychoanalytic theory, which I propose to term ‘possession anxiety’. Possession anxiety relates to the presence of an ambivalently charged object, which can take its power from the person possessing it. The person will then fear losing control over the object. Possession anxiety is a normal phenomenon, though it is most evident in sexual perversions and anorexia nervosa. It is symbolically represented by the phallus and is associated to the genital stage of psychosexual development.

I briefly examine this concept from the viewpoint of its temporal connotations and in its psychotherapeutic significance for the understanding of the transference. I use as illustration fragments from child observation and from my clinical work with analytic patients.

General Practitioner Attachments and the Multidisciplinary Team

David Jones

David Jones

David Jones  

The relationship between professionals of different disciplines in the Health and Social Services has long been problematical. Issues of control and responsibility have concerned medical and non-medical staff alike. The establishment of generic social work departments, post Seebohm, has gone some way towards equalising the power balance as far as social workers are concerned. However, although the independence that they thereby acquired has arguably been beneficial to their working practices and to their identity as a separate professional group, it would be misleading to suggest that this has made the basic problem disappear. Indeed it might be contended that the underlying emotional issues have only been avoided and still have to be dealt with by each individual worker in the field. More recently it has become apparent that the nursing profession has been trying to come to terms with some of the same issues by organisational means.

For three years I was able to work with a team at Littlemore Hospital, Oxford, which comprised social workers, senior and junior psychiatrists, psychologists, two psychiatric nurses and a hospital chaplin who is also a trained analyst. The specific focus of this team was the G. P. attachment which each team member undertook. This brings us immediately to another important area since the relationship of outsider to general practitioner does itself require delicate negotiation. However it will be useful to describe the setting in which the team was based.

The Setting

The Ashhurst clinic is part of Littlemore Hospital in Oxford. The building itself is divided into a small in-patient unit, some administrative and social work offices and a day unit. It is to the last of these, the day unit, that I am referring.

The day unit offers an intensive three-day-a-week programme to individuals who present with problems ranging from borderline psychosis to severe emotional difficulties expressed as problems with living. The programme is designed to be rigorous but also holding and caring.

Joel Ryce-Menuhin

Joel Ryce-Menuhin

Joel Ryce-Menuhin  

Madame Chasseguet-Smirgel has written an important book. In reviewing it I will try to reveal its essence rather than elaborating further its rich detail. Chasseguet-Smirgel presents in this work the clearest conceptualisation of the ego ideal and the newest theory as to its functions that this reviewer has found in the psychoanalytic literature.

Her theoretical perspective is of interest to Jungians because she does not see the ego as present at birth, as did Melanie Klein, but sees the initial fusion to mother as-self as the seat of that time when the baby was his own ideal. The nostalgia for this time, when delusion to mother has not yet occurred, prompts narcissism to function on the subject's own behalf. In this memory of what Freudians name ‘primary narcissism’ and what Jungians consider as an ‘initial wholeself affirmation’, the ego-ideal can be maturative in its attempt to integrate its own levels of development and to reconquer (theoretically) the lost perfection of fusion.

Identification with objects that carry the subject's narcissism is not, then, Chasseguet-Smirgel's definition of the ego-ideal as it has been among many neoFreudians. Instead she postulates a theory of the ego-ideal in which the ego tries to reduce the margins between its identifications with different models during maturation (including the infantile sexual stages) and thereby comes closer to its ‘ideal’ goal. The author discusses the ego's narcissistic satisfaction when it comes nearer to its ideal through discovering its real capacities and object relations in an ongoing process.

Although the incestuous and grandiose aims of the ego-ideal are recognised by the author, she stresses that the aims toward instant gratification, on her theory, are learned over time as the all-or-nothing quality of ego-omnipotence is given a freer, looser play and eventually abandoned during the formation of the superego. With the superego's development, narcissism transfers away from self-incestuous fantasies to the service of the superego. This implies that the agent of reality becomes the superego which breaks up the Oedipal complex with the child's recognition that genital primacy is the father's prerogative, not only because it is forbidden to the child but because the child realises he doesn't himself have the necessary capability. This can lead in adulthood to a positive development when the subject reconciles the dormant former wishes of Oedipal fulfilment with the demands of his superego. This is achieved by loving (with the sublimations involved) a person in spite of their finiteness and just because of this limit, learning to live the trials and creative and procreative act involves within the subject's entire ego-world.

Robert Royston

Robert Royston

Robert Royston  

Given Janine Chassequet-Smirgel's standing in French psychoanalysis this book would appear a coup for the newly-established Free Association Books. Otto Kernberg, who writes a foreword, speaks of her ‘creative exploration of the intersection of some of the most challenging and complex areas of psychoanalytic inquiry: perversion, narcissism and aggression, particularly as these relate to artistic creativity, group psychology and political ideology’. Kernberg's appetite for more, he tells us, has been whetted.

Yet Adam Mars Jones, reviewing in a London Sunday paper, dismissed the book with irritated distaste as un-rigorous, poorly written and guilty of precisely the destructive homogenisation the author discerns in the perversions.

Who is right? Mars Jones won the Somerset Maugham Award in 1982 for his story collection Lantern Lecture. Is he prejudiced against psychoanalysis? Was he insulted by the highly unflattering portrait of the artist which emerges from Chasseguet-Smirgel's pages? Is he psychophobic? Is Kernberg uncritical and indulgent to a member of his tribe? Or is there an irreconcilable intellectual conflict between psychoanalysis and the rest of the community?

But first the book's main themes. Creativity and Perversion's much reiterated central theory postulates a universal temptation to a perversion that does not necessarily involve sexual symptoms. Both this and the explicit sexual abberrations begin at the threshold of the Oedipal stage. Here the child must acknowledge the primacy of the father, his superior adult penis and his ‘genital universe’ - the real world where nothing is achieved through sham or fantasy but through struggle and realism. But, aided by a seductive, pampering mother, the child may shun humility and a necessary identification with his father, reject a whole maturational phase, and see himself as already adult and potent and a suitable partner for mother.

The recent presentation of audiovisual tapes in Switzerland by Drs. Davanloo and Malan was designed to introduce to the uninitiated the techniques of dynamic psychotherapy developed over the years by Dr. Davanloo during his work in Montreal. The first two days were concerned with tapes of the initial interview with the patient and with early sessions during the subsequent therapy. On the third day tapes of follow-up sessions were shown, up to nine years after termination; in these, the patient was invited to watch and comment upon extracts from the tapes of his therapy. We were also shown the tape of a female patient whose therapy had been extended when it became known that her father was terminally ill.

Dr. Habib Davanloo was born in Persia into a family of the professional class. He trained as a surgeon before emigrating to the United States in the 1950s, without knowing a word of English, and worked for some time as a surgeon in New York. After working with Lindemann, he became interested in psychoanalysis and trained as an analyst. Disillusionment over the length of time needed to carry out a full-scale analysis led him to develop his own technique in conjunction with rigorous research procedures as to its effectiveness. Dr. David Malan, the leading exponent of short-term dynamic psychotherapy in this country and the man who has completed the most research on this form of psychotherapy, has been working closely with Dr. Davanloo for a number of years, insofar as the distance between Montreal, where the latter is based, and the Tavistock Clinic will permit.

The techniques employed by Dr. Davanloo are firmly rooted in the standard psychoanalytic principles underlying all dynamic psychotherapy. These may be understood most easily with the aid of the Malan-Menninger triangles described by David Malan (1979).

The author is Registrar in Psychiatry at Littlemore Hospital, Littlemore, Oxford.

Clinical Commentary

(A short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the history of the case. The material has been sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention in putting these commentaries side by side is to compare the approaches of the different schools in order to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice.)

The Therapist Writes

The Patient

G. is a young man in his early twenties but looks about seventeen. He has a rather beautiful, sensual, sensitive face - and some years ago found great pleasure in ‘natural dance’. He told me at our first meeting that he needed therapy because he had ‘killed all his feelings’. He now experiences the world as unreal, his body feels dead and numb. At worst he fears being suicidal or going mad.

Recent history. About six months before meeting me he had ‘clamped himself down’. He said he had been very wrong to do it. It was in a sense a chosen course to take. He wished he could have come to me six months earlier and wondered if it would be possible to reverse the damage. He had left university in the second year. He had been studying engineering. Having failed his first-year exams he opted out of retaking them and returned home to live with his parents. He took a low-paid clerical job in which he could survive in a mechanical way while living in dreamland. He had chosen to kill off his feelings as an escape from the pain and fear of experiencing other people and the outside world. It is as if he lacked a necessary protective layer between himself and the outside world, and to kill his feelings had been his only defence. He said that at school he hadn't been able to imagine how he would live when he had left - and had thought he might commit suicide.

Family background. G. is an only child. His father was seriously depressed all through G's childhood. He remembers his father as withdrawn, inaccessible, requiring peace, quiet - and not to be disturbed. His mother he describes as ‘capable, cheerful, and with no problems luckily’. His mother kept things going, and G. said he never experienced or needed any aggression as a child. It appears that he and his mother lived in a close, loving, mutually supportive relationship - while looking after father in his depressed state. Speaking of his struggle at university, G. said he never realised that life was so hard and you needed to push yourself. He feels that he has no aggression or anger in him.

Kleinian Developments in the Concept of Narcissism

Penelope Elder

Penelope Elder

24 Muswell Road, Muswell Hill, London N10 2BG

Penelope Elder  

In this paper I want to explore some of the more recent ideas regarding the concept of narcissism as it has been described and developed since the early part of this century when three papers gave a particular focus to the subject: Freud's ‘On Narcissism: An Introduction’ (1914), Jones's paper on pathological narcissistic character traits ‘The God Complex’ 1913), and Abraham's paper ‘A Particular Form of Neurotic Resistance against the Psychoanalytic Method’ (1919).

Even before 1914 Freud had introduced the concept of the existence of a stage in sexual development between auto-erotism and object love. The subject ‘begins by taking himself, his own body, as his love-object’. But it is his paper ‘On Narcissism’ which integrates the notion into psychoanalytic theory as a whole. He puts forward the idea that the ego does not exist from the very first as a unity and that a ‘new psychical action’ has to take place in order to bring about narcissism.

Freud maintains an opposition between a first, objectless narcissistic state and object relations. This primitive state, now called ‘Primary Narcissism’, is supposed to be characterised by the total absence of any relationship to the outside world and by a lack of differentiation between ego and id. He seems however to modify his views on this in ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ where he speaks of that state as being a ‘narcissistic identification with the object’. The idea of a narcissism contemporaneous with the formation of the ego through identification with the other person - ‘Secondary Narcissism’ - was put forward in 1923 in ‘The Ego and the Id’ as ‘the libido which flows into the ego owing to the identification with the object’. The narcissism of the ego is thus a secondary one which has been withdrawn from objects. ‘Secondary Narcissism’ can be defined as the love of the self which results from introjecting and identifying with an object.

In fact Freud adopted some of Abraham's ideas in relating narcissism to libidinal cathexes, showing what withdrawal of libido from the object or the outside world on to the ego is very much a symptom of psychoses. He postulates a see-saw balance between egolibido (love directed towards the self) and objectlibido: ‘the more the one is employed, the more the other becomes depleted’. This is particularly shown in his understanding of hypochondria and paraphrenia (schizophrenia), in the withdrawal of interest from external reality and preoccupation with the subject's own inner world.
